Start with a repeatable request

Keep the brief about the workflow.

Keep confidential records out of the virtual assistant task planner. Your virtual assistant task brief can describe the systems and types of information the work needs.

  • Use an invented example or remove personal information from an existing example.
  • Leave passwords, private links and customer records out of the brief.
  • Describe the permission needed for the task, such as viewing a queue or editing drafts.

See the first handoff process

Write the brief around the result.

Use the virtual assistant task planner to choose a specific result. A virtual assistant task brief for inbox work will differ from one for a content release.

Inbox or calendar

Ask for a short daily brief that shows what needs a decision, which messages can wait and which meetings have changed. Describe how to handle a private item or a change outside the agreed calendar rules.

Customer or lead queue

Ask for requests to be checked, assigned and updated in the tool your team already uses. Include one exception and say who can approve a refund, merge a record or change the next action.

Content or website

Ask for an approved draft to be checked, scheduled or prepared for review. Define which assets are current, which fields are in scope and who approves a live release.

Describe a window someone can plan around.

Include timing in your virtual assistant task brief. The virtual assistant requirements template can record a regular review window and a deadline for urgent work.

Specify when work arrives

Note the days and channels that usually produce requests. If work comes in after hours, say whether it should wait for the next window or be escalated.

Explain what is urgent

Give an example of an urgent request and a routine one. Write down who can move other work to make room for the urgent item and where that decision should be recorded.

Show typical volume

Estimate a normal week and call out peaks such as launches or reporting deadlines. The person reviewing the brief can then decide whether the initial scope needs one task or a larger queue.

Read the brief as the person who will use it.

Read your virtual assistant task brief as the next person to act. Use the virtual assistant task planner to clarify the source, output and decision owner.

Can they find the starting point?

Identify where work arrives and which type of request belongs in the task. If two systems are involved, state which one records the final result.

Can they tell when the task is finished?

Include a realistic outcome and a reviewer. For instance, a finished page update could require a preview, checked links and a record of final approval.

Can they recognise an exception?

Name the situations that need a different route and the role that makes the decision. Check whether the brief explains who should act if the normal owner is away.

Test one normal item and one exception.

Use a normal request to check the virtual assistant requirements template. Your virtual assistant task brief should also explain what happens when that rule cannot apply.

Start with the normal route

Check whether the source, expected result and deadline are clear without filling in gaps from memory. Add any missing detail to the brief.

Try the exception

Ask who would decide and what the assistant would send to them. If the answer depends on the person available that day, name a backup route.

Update the virtual assistant requirements template

Record the change and keep the latest version with the work. Review another example after the new instruction has been used.

Turn a broad request into a usable task.

Use the virtual assistant task planner to break a broad goal into clear steps. Your virtual assistant task brief should let someone identify the first action.

Start with the actual request

Name the mailbox, the types of messages to check and when the work should happen. Include any folders or senders your team uses to identify requests. For example, ask for a weekday review of routine appointment requests and outstanding replies.

Describe what to return

Ask for one summary that lists urgent messages, routine replies ready for approval and items waiting on another person. Give an example of how each row should appear so the first draft is easy to compare.

Make exceptions concrete

Name one case that needs your decision, such as a new appointment that conflicts with an existing commitment. Add who can approve a change and when they should hear about it.

Fill in the details you have today.

Start the virtual assistant requirements template with the details available today. Use the virtual assistant task planner to identify questions your team still needs to answer.

When volume varies

Describe a normal day and a busy day using a recent range. If there is no count yet, share how requests arrive and the event that tends to increase them. The first test can produce a better estimate.

When the tool is undecided

State where the work is handled today and where you want to see the finished result. Ask the current owner to check whether the assistant can use the existing queue and what access it would require.

When someone else owns approval

List the role that should make the decision and when it is normally available. Confirm the individual and backup with your team before the task depends on that approval.

Improve your virtual assistant task brief

Update the virtual assistant task brief after reviewing a sample result. Your virtual assistant requirements template should reflect the revised instruction for the next request.

Check the missing context

If the assistant could not classify a request, add the field or example they needed. Make the rule concrete enough that the same request would have a clear next step the next time it arrives.

Check the output

If the result took time to review, show which part was hard to use. Agree where decision requests should sit and what supporting links should be included so the reviewer can move faster.

Check the approval

If work stalled with an unanswered question, update the decision owner or review window. Use the revised brief on a similar task and record whether it resolved the delay.

Frequently Asked Questions

Review your virtual assistant task brief before submitting an enquiry. A short description is enough when the expected result and approvals are clear.

Can I ask about more than one service?

Yes. Describe the work you need help with and tell us which task should come first. Include any other teams or workflows that depend on it.

Can I enquire if I’m still defining the role?

Yes. Start with the work that keeps piling up and the result you want. Include the tools you use or the hours you need covered if you know them.

Do I need every field to get started?

Yes. Enter your name, company name, email and phone number, then describe the work you need help with.

What makes a task description useful?

A virtual assistant task brief should name what arrives, what action is needed and what should come back. Use one recent request and include a case that needs a different decision so the reviewer can understand the limits.

What if I do not know the exact workload?

Use a typical day and a busy day to describe the range. The virtual assistant requirements template can record approximate volume, when requests arrive and the deadlines your team has already promised.

Can I include private customer information?

Use an invented or anonymised example to explain the task. Keep passwords, confidential records and private links out of the enquiry, and agree an approved channel for any information the actual work will require.

Make room for the work only you can do.

Tell us which task you’d like to hand off and what a good result looks like. Start with one piece of work that comes up regularly.
